Normal: Reliability Monitor shows recent failures. Open it (search 'Reliability Monitor' in Start) to see exactly which app or driver is failing.
Bad: The system is failing frequently. Open Reliability Monitor to identify the repeating failure, and check the other Stability findings in this report for the root cause.

Normal: A few corrected hardware errors were logged — usually harmless, but re-check monthly for growth.
Bad: Frequent corrected hardware errors suggest a component running at its margin.
If RAM-related: turn OFF the XMP/EXPO memory overclock in BIOS first — it is the most common cause.
Check CPU/GPU temperatures and the PSU; run Windows Memory Diagnostic (it requires a reboot).

rules.forecast: Corrected errors that trend upward often become uncorrectable errors — the component is degrading.

Bad: Uncorrectable hardware errors were logged — failing CPU, RAM, or motherboard territory. BACK UP YOUR FILES FIRST.
Turn off any overclocking (XMP/EXPO included), update the BIOS, and run Windows Memory Diagnostic.
If errors continue at stock settings, have the hardware tested/replaced.

Normal: One or two unexpected shutdowns in 90 days — fine if they match real power cuts or a held power button. Re-check next month.
Bad: Frequent unexpected shutdowns point to power delivery (failing PSU, loose cable, weak wall power) or overheating.
Laptops: check the battery health finding. Desktops: reseat power cables; consider testing with a known-good PSU.
Check CPU/GPU temperatures under load — thermal shutdowns log the same event.

rules.forecast: Unexpected power loss also corrupts files and damages SSD data in flight — every occurrence is a small data-loss risk.

Normal: One blue screen in 90 days — note the stop code if it happens again; repeats matter, single events mostly don't.
Bad: Repeated blue screens. Update drivers (GPU first), uninstall recently added software/drivers, and run Windows Memory Diagnostic.
If crash dumps are enabled (see the crash-dump finding), the dump files identify the failing driver.

Normal: A couple of display-driver resets — often a driver bug. Install the latest (or roll back to the previous stable) GPU driver.
Bad: Frequent GPU driver resets: clean-install the latest GPU driver (DDU in safe mode is the thorough way).
If it persists across driver versions: check GPU temperatures, remove any GPU overclock, and make sure PSU power cables to the card are fully seated.
Persisting at stock settings with good temps = the GPU itself may be failing.

Normal: A handful of app crashes this week. If it's the same app every time, reinstall/update that app.
Bad: Many crashes across different apps usually mean a system-level cause: run Windows Memory Diagnostic and check the disk findings.
Also run 'sfc /scannow' from an admin prompt to check system files.

Normal: Open Device Manager, find the flagged device (details list it), and update or reinstall its driver.
Bad: Several devices report driver problems — run Windows Update (it delivers drivers too), then fix the rest in Device Manager from the vendor's site.

Normal: Crash dumps are disabled, so blue screens can't be diagnosed afterwards. Enable 'Automatic memory dump' in SystemPropertiesAdvanced > Startup and Recovery.
No page file is configured — crash dumps can't be written and memory pressure can kill apps. Set it back to 'Automatically manage' in SystemPropertiesAdvanced > Performance settings.
